title: Dynamics-Aware Sampling and Recovery for Tensor-Valued Dynamical Systems
abstract: We study sampling and recovery for tensor-valued dynamical systems evolving under the t-product, using partial spatial observations over time. Although the t-product Fourier transform yields slicewise matrix dynamics, recovery does not generally decouple across slices. Eigenvalues shared across Fourier-domain frontal slices couple the corresponding eigenspaces into aggregated spectral blocks, which determine the tensor-specific recovery geometry and space--time tradeoff. We establish deterministic identifiability conditions for the initial tensor state. In the diagonalizable case, these are frame conditions on the aggregated blocks. We extend them to non-diagonalizable systems through generalized eigenspaces and Jordan structure. A temporal--spectral factorization of the finite-horizon stacked recovery system underlying Tensor Dynamical Sampling (DS) yields a decoupled two-stage formulation once the temporal threshold is reached. Under independent spatial subsampling, we prove high-probability recovery guarantees using empirical Gram matrices on the aggregated blocks. The bounds depend on aggregated multiplicities, incoherence, and population conditioning. Stability estimates separate the spatial frame factor from the temporal Vandermonde factor and show that increasing temporal depth may worsen numerical conditioning even after identifiability is ensured. We implement Tensor DS and evaluate it on synthetic and real data. Phase transitions track the predicted blockwise sampling thresholds, and stability experiments illustrate Vandermonde conditioning. Experiments on sea surface temperature and turbulence velocity data show that a learned t-product system operator generally yields more accurate and structurally faithful reconstructions than vectorized low-rank, Tucker-type, graph-regularized, graph-spectral, and vectorized dynamical sampling baselines.

title: At FullTilt: Real-Time Open-Set 3D Macromolecule Detection Directly from Tilted 2D Projections
abstract: Open-set 3D macromolecule detection in cryogenic electron tomography eliminates the need for target-specific model retraining. However, strict VRAM constraints prohibit processing an entire 3D tomogram, forcing current methods to rely on slow sliding-window inference over extracted subvolumes. To overcome this, we propose FullTilt, an end-to-end framework that redefines 3D detection by operating directly on aligned 2D tilt-series. Because a tilt-series contains significantly fewer images than slices in a reconstructed tomogram, FullTilt eliminates redundant volumetric computation, accelerating inference by orders of magnitude. To process the entire tilt-series simultaneously, we introduce a tilt-series encoder to efficiently fuse cross-view information. We further propose a multiclass visual prompt encoder for flexible prompting, a tilt-aware query initializer to effectively anchor 3D queries, and an auxiliary geometric primitives module to enhance the model's understanding of multi-view geometry while improving robustness to adverse imaging artifacts. Extensive evaluations on three real-world datasets demonstrate that FullTilt achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance while drastically reducing runtime and VRAM requirements, paving the way for rapid, large-scale visual proteomics analysis. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Kaminyou/FullTilt.

title: How High Can GPT-6 Astra Climb in Contact-Rich Manipulation? PhysLadder: A Hierarchical, Matched Sim-Real Benchmark for Physical Interaction
abstract: We introduce PhysLadder, a hierarchical Sim-Real benchmark for evaluating physical interaction capabilities in contact-rich manipulation. Its 16 household tasks span three cumulative levels: contact selection and geometric alignment (L1), force regulation within sustained contact (L2), and coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation (L3). Each task is instantiated in physically and visually matched simulated and real-world environments, with shared task definitions and success criteria. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra zero-shot with three trials per task in each environment. Real-world success rates decline from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2 and 0.0% at L3, with corresponding simulation rates of 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%. Ten of the 16 tasks have identical success counts across environments; the remaining six differ by one success out of three trials. Across both environments, recurring difficulties in spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordination often prevent local physical progress from accumulating into task completion. These findings characterize Astra's observed capability boundary across increasing interaction demands and, for this model, support matched simulation as a repeatable, scalable testbed for studying the sustained, coordinated physical interactions that limit reliable manipulation.

title: Spectra, Growth, and Localization in Half-Bounded Tensor Triangular Geometry
abstract: Over a noetherian scheme, classical cohomological support determines thick tensor ideals of perfect complexes. In half-bounded derived categories, complexes with the same support can generate different radical thick tensor ideals. We study how these distinctions affect the Balmer spectrum and localization. For a commutative noetherian ring $R$, we prove that $\operatorname{Spc}(\mathbf D^-_{\mathrm{fg}}(R))$ is noetherian if and only if $R$ is artinian. For a nonempty noetherian scheme $X$, the corresponding condition is $\dim X=0$. For such a ring $R$ and a finite group $G$, $\operatorname{Spc}(\mathbf D^-_{\mathrm{fg}}(RG))$ is noetherian if and only if $R$ is artinian and $|G|$ is invertible in $R$. Using the Sanders--Zhang classification over a discrete valuation ring, we compare objects whose annihilator exponents grow at different rates in different degrees. We lift the relevant generation relations before changing coefficients and obtain spectral retractions. These comparisons persist after thick quotients and algebraic localization under explicit uniform annihilation and nonvanishing conditions. A second argument uses nonnilpotent classes of positive degree and passes from cyclic subgroups to finite groups. Applications include relative results for schemes and bounded-below spectra with degreewise finitely generated homotopy. We also describe the cohomological information shared by the resulting ideals. The localization comparisons for bounded-below complexes of finitely generated modules and for bounded-below derived objects with finitely generated cohomology are established separately.

title: Amplitude-Dependent Damping of Gravity--Capillary Waves in Power-Law Fluids: An Energy-Dissipation Framework
abstract: Classical gravity--capillary theory locates the restoring-force crossover, but the wave amplitudes and depths for which energy losses remain measurable depend on the constitutive response and on where viscous dissipation occurs. We develop a weak-loss mechanical-energy model for small-steepness progressive surface waves in memoryless power--law liquids. The full invariant of the leading inviscid strain field yields the deep-water bulk law $\dd A/\dd t=-C_tA^n$, with $C_t=4Kk^2(2kΩ)^{n-1}/[(n+1)ρ]$, and the corresponding spatial law $\dd A/\dd x=-(C_t/v_g)A^n$. For finite depth we calculate bulk dissipation using a phase- and depth-resolved quadrature $J_n(kh)$ and formulate a separate oscillatory power--law bottom layer. We solve the latter numerically in periodic state, obtaining dimensionless integrated wall losses $I_{0.6}\simeq0.5432$ and $I_{1.4}\simeq0.4708$ and recovering the exact Newtonian benchmark $I_1=1/2$. These values make it possible to evaluate conditional finite-depth bulk--wall dominance boundaries rather than only their amplitude exponents. The theory is organized into restoring-force, attenuation, local propagation-length, and dissipation-mechanism regime maps; at fixed wave steepness it additionally predicts a capillary-side maximum of normalized temporal damping for $0<n<2/3$. Grid, time-step, domain, and energy-work checks support the reduced wall calculation, while the coupled bulk--wall approximation still requires independent free-surface numerical or experimental validation. The results provide a reproducible single-fluid reference for subsequent two-liquid interfacial-wave modeling.

title: U-VLM: Hierarchical Vision Language Modeling for Report Generation
abstract: Automated radiology report generation is key for reducing radiologist workload and improving diagnostic consistency, yet generating accurate reports for 3D medical imaging remains challenging. Existing vision-language models face two limitations: they do not leverage segmentation-pretrained encoders, and they inject visual features only at the input layer of language models, losing multi-scale information. We propose U-VLM, which enables hierarchical vision-language modeling in both training and architecture: (1) progressive training from segmentation to classification to report generation, and (2) multi-layer visual injection that routes U-Net encoder features to corresponding language model layers. Each training stage can leverage different datasets without unified annotations. U-VLM achieves state-of-the-art performance on CT-RATE (F1: 0.414 vs 0.258, BLEU-mean: 0.349 vs 0.305) and AbdomenAtlas 3.0 (F1: 0.624 vs 0.518 for segmentation-based detection) using only a 0.1B decoder trained from scratch, demonstrating that well-designed vision encoder pretraining outweighs the benefits of 7B+ pre-trained language models. Ablation studies show that progressive pretraining significantly improves F1, while multi-layer injection improves BLEU-mean. Code is available at https://github.com/yinghemedical/U-VLM.

title: DAOS: A Multimodal In-cabin Behavior Monitoring with Driver Action-Object Synergy Dataset
abstract: Multimodal action understanding requires complementary sensory observations to be connected with structured semantic knowledge. This is particularly challenging in vehicle cabins, where fine-grained actions exhibit similar upper-body motion, relevant objects may be small or occluded, and appearance varies substantially across illumination conditions. Existing in-cabin datasets, however, rarely provide synchronized visual modalities together with dense object annotations and explicit action--object alignment, limiting the study of object-grounded multimodal recognition. To address this gap, we introduce the Driver Action with Object Synergy (DAOS) dataset, containing 9,787 video clips, 36 fine-grained actions, 15 object categories, and more than 2.5 million annotated object instances. DAOS provides synchronized RGB, infrared, and depth observations from four camera views, thereby combining complementary appearance, low-light, and geometric information. Building on DAOS, we propose the Action-Object-Relation Network (AOR-Net), a vision-language framework that organizes multimodal understanding at three semantic levels: action, object, and human-object relation. Its Chain-of-action Prompting mechanism progressively grounds global motion with localized object and relation cues, while a textual prototype bank supplies corresponding semantic descriptions. A Mixture of Thoughts module then dynamically selects and integrates the most informative semantic levels and visual modalities under object-rich and object-scarce conditions. Extensive experiments show that AOR-Net consistently outperforms strong baselines on DAOS, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining heterogeneous visual sensing with structured action-object-relation semantics for fine-grained multimodal video understanding.

title: Robust Observability for Schrödinger Equations with Singular Potentials on 2D Compact Hyperbolic Surfaces
abstract: This paper investigates the robustness of quantum observability on compact hyperbolic surfaces subject to $L^q$ potential perturbations with $2<q\leq \infty$. Since $L^q$ regularity is strictly subcritical in dimension two, for every non-empty open set $Ω\subset M$ and $T>0$, the solution of $(i\partial_t+Δ-V)u=0$ satisfies the space-time observability estimate $$ \|u_0\|_{L^2(M)}^2 \leq C\int_0^T \|e^{-it(-Δ+V)}u_0\|_{L^2(Ω)}^2\,dt. $$ A cornerstone of our analysis is Sogge's spectral cluster estimate, which allows us to obtain refined spectrally localized semiclassical Strichartz estimates adapted to rough potentials and to show that the potential's contribution vanishes in the propagation of semiclassical measures. The full-support property of invariant semiclassical measures on hyperbolic surfaces associated with the eigenfunctions then yields the desired observability by contradiction. By the Hilbert Uniqueness Method, the corresponding internal controllability result follows.

title: Recovering fractal boundary dimensions from Robin eigenvalues
abstract: We study Robin problems in which a small local boundary coefficient competes with the increasing surface measure of a finite-depth fractal approximation. For a fixed smooth domain, layer potentials give Green function and eigenpair expansions; contour residues and a finite-rank reduction yield a quantitative spectral-gap-dependent eigenvalue remainder. For varying Lipschitz domains, a uniform Poincaré inequality and a trace estimate with respect to normalized surface measure give a uniform ground-state expansion and a rank-one resolvent singularity as the total Robin boundary mass tends to zero. Under the boundary-resolution hypothesis and the condition on the approximation scales, ground-state measurements with known Robin coefficients recover the lower and upper Minkowski dimensions for sequences with bounded total Robin boundary mass. We describe Neumann, generalized Robin, and Dirichlet-type operator limits under the corresponding compact Mosco convergence hypotheses. Koch snowflake computations illustrate the reconstruction formulas, and an exact finite-stage area correction improves the adjacent-stage dimension estimator.

title: Forecasting Ionospheric Irregularities on GNSS Lines of Sight Using Dynamic Graphs with Ephemeris Conditioning
abstract: Most data-driven ionospheric models operate on gridded products, which do not preserve the time-varying sampling structure of satellite-based sensing. We instead model the ionosphere as a dynamic graph over ionospheric pierce points, with connectivity that evolves as satellite positions change. Because satellite trajectories are predictable, the graph topology over the forecast horizon can be constructed in advance. We exploit this property to condition forecasts on the future graph structure, which we term ephemeris conditioning. This enables prediction on lines of sight (LoS) that appear only in the forecast horizon. We evaluate our framework on Global Navigation Satellite System data from a co-located receiver pair in Singapore spanning 2023 to 2025. The task is forecasting irregularities defined by the Rate of TEC Index (ROTI) up to 2 hours ahead as per-node binary classification. The resulting model, IonoDGNN, achieves a Brier Skill Score (BSS) of 0.55 and an area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC) of 0.77. These correspond to improvements over persistence of 53% in BSS and 58% in PR-AUC, with larger gains at longer lead times. Ablations confirm that graph structure and ephemeris conditioning each contribute meaningfully. Under simulated coverage dropout, the model retains predictive skill on affected nodes through spatial message passing from observed neighbors. Compared to interpolation baselines, the proposed model achieves better recovery, especially at higher dropout levels. These results suggest that dynamic graph forecasting on evolving LoS is a viable alternative for ionospheric modeling. The project and the dataset are available at https://github.com/Mert-chan/IonoDGNN.

title: Perturbative Coulomb branches on $\mathbb{R}^3\times S^1$: the global D-term potential
abstract: We develop a Wilsonian description of perturbative D-terms in 4d $\mathcal N=1$ gauge theories on $\mathbb R^3\times S^1$ with chiral Kaluza--Klein spectra. A closed-form, one-loop-exact coefficient of the auxiliary D fields, including 4d Fayet--Iliopoulos parameters and globally valid throughout the holonomy space, determines the leading holonomy potential away from massless thresholds. We establish uniform weak-coupling control there and match across thresholds by retaining the light fields. Gauge-anomaly cancellation renders the Coulomb-slice vacuum equations affine within each chamber bounded by the thresholds, enabling exact linear analysis of their zero sets and numerical reconstruction through DBSCAN clustering of approximate zeros, LPCA denoising, and RANSAC hyperplane detection. Complementing the rank-one applications of the accompanying Letter, we study flavor-twist dependence in the $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ $\mathcal N=4$ theory, and illustrate the numerical reconstruction in higher-rank R-twisted Argyres--Douglas reductions of interest in the SCFT/VOA correspondence. We also relate the same D-term data to leading stationary-phase equations of supersymmetric partition functions and a decompactification limit of the torus twisted superpotential.

title: Bistable fronts in periodic media: phase reduction and realization of circle flows
abstract: We establish a phase reduction and a converse realization theorem for front dynamics in one-dimensional periodic reaction-diffusion-advection equations. For sufficiently large periods under local bistability, and sufficiently small periods when the homogenized equation admits a stationary front, we construct strictly ordered invariant front families that are normally exponentially attracting and locally complete for entire orbits. Modulo spatial-period translations, the dynamics on each family reduces exactly to a circle flow: rotations correspond to propagating pulsating fronts, equilibria to stationary fronts, and connecting orbits to transition fronts between stationary fronts. Conversely, every smooth circle flow can be realized, up to time-preserving topological conjugacy, as the quotient dynamics of such a family for a periodic, locally bistable equation with constant diffusion and no advection. Realizations with a Cantor set of stationary phases and a connecting orbit in each complementary interval illustrate the richness of front dynamics in these media. We also obtain first-order phase-velocity expansions in both period limits, quantitative propagation laws near zero frozen speed, and global exponential orbital stability of propagating pulsating fronts.

title: From Slices to Volumes: Comparing 2D, 2.5D, and 3D Residual Networks for Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy-Risk Classification
abstract: Purpose: To compare 2D, 2.5D, and 3D residual networks for pulmonary nodule malignancy-risk classification and evaluate momentum-contrast pretraining, mild augmentation, and exclusion of indeterminate ratings. Methods: A retrospectively prepared LIDC-IDRI cohort contained 2,654 nodules labeled benign, indeterminate, or malignant using median radiologist ratings. Patient-disjoint splits comprised 1,876 training, 382 validation, and 396 test nodules. Representations included one axial slice, five neighboring slices, and a local CT volume. Each track evaluated a randomly initialized baseline, momentum-contrast pretraining followed by fine-tuning, and supervised training with mild augmentation. Checkpoints were selected by validation Macro-F1. The 2D experiments used three seeds; 2.5D and 3D results were single-run estimates. A separate binary experiment excluded indeterminate nodules. Results: Augmented models achieved test Macro-F1 values of $0.6134\pm0.0075$ for 2D, $0.6537$ for 2.5D, and $0.5403$ for 3D; the 2D uncertainty denotes population standard deviation across seeds. Corresponding accuracies were $0.6128$, $0.6869$, and $0.5455$. Augmentation improved Macro-F1 within every track, whereas the tested pretraining recipes reduced it. Binary Macro-F1 values were $0.8227$, $0.8664$, and $0.7554$, respectively. Conclusion: Augmented 2.5D achieved the highest observed performance. Differences in preprocessing, optimization, capacity, and replication limit attribution to dimensionality. Labels reflect radiologist-assessed malignancy risk rather than pathology-confirmed cancer. Code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/CT-DeepLearning-Team/CT-2D-2.5D-3D-DeepLearning.

title: AudioFM: Towards General Purpose Audio Representation Learning
abstract: Learning audio representations that effectively bridge holistic global soundscapes with fine-grained acoustic moments is a long-standing goal in self-supervised learning. Recording-level contrastive objectives encourage agreement between pooled audio representations, but do not explicitly supervise local time-frequency representations. We introduce AudioFM, a self-supervised framework that combines recording-level contrast with patch-wise masked latent discrimination. Using visible acoustic context, a student predicts representations of masked patches and identifies their corresponding full-view teacher targets among candidates from other recordings. We further incorporate weaker supervision from eligible temporal neighbors to encourage local temporal consistency. Extensive evaluations show that AudioFM achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse audio domains in linear probing, fine-tuning, and zero-shot transfer, demonstrating superior event detection, robust scene-level understanding, and strong domain generalizability.

title: Structured Continuity Equations in Fibred Wasserstein Spaces
abstract: In this article, we develop a comprehensive ODE-theory for structured continuity equations in fibred probability spaces, which represent a class of heterogeneous PDEs arising as the meanfield limit of nonexchangeable particle systems. After investigating in depth the topologies induced by the so-called fibred (or conditional) and classical Wasserstein metrics on such probability spaces, we establish quantitative Cauchy-Lipschitz and qualitative Carathéodory-Peano well-posedness results for structured continuity equations, along with precise correspondences between this class of evolutions, classical Lagrangian dynamics, and continuity equations. In keeping with what has long been known for exchangeable dynamics, we derive a general meanfield approximation result by solutions of nonexchangeable particle systems, along with a quantitative variant thereof under practically reasonable regularity assumptions on the driving field and initial data.

title: Functional Superoscillations in a Wave Processor
abstract: Physical wave processors are constrained by diffraction, but the bandwidth of the mathematical functions they implement need not be set by it. Here, we demonstrate continuous and multiplexed optical processing of superoscillatory functions, in which a scalar argument is encoded onto a wavefront and a fixed diffractive wave processor synthesizes optical responses that approximate the corresponding function outputs in parallel. Unlike conventional superoscillatory optics that generates predetermined fields, superoscillation here is expressed in the input-output dependence on the encoded argument. Its frequencies are therefore distinct from the transverse spatial frequencies of propagating light and are not subject to the same diffraction-imposed cutoff. We demonstrate complex-valued superoscillatory function synthesis and introduce a multiplexed architecture that simultaneously evaluates distinct target superoscillatory functions whose harmonic content exceeds that of the optical input encoding. Visible-light experiments further validate this beyond-encoding superoscillatory regime. Together, these results establish functional superoscillation as a design principle for wave-based computation and show how interference, diffractive depth and spatial channel allocation extend the functional reach of passive wave processors. More broadly, these analyses establish a separation between functional bandwidth and physical wave bandwidth in analog optical computation.

title: Bi-Objective Receding-Horizon Scheduling of Nurses and Hospital Service Robots
abstract: This paper studies the joint scheduling of nurses and hospital service robots as a bi-objective mixed-integer linear programming problem. The formulation represents heterogeneous nursing skills, alternative skill-coverage modes, nurse availability and temporal rules, workload balance, robot task capability, charging and battery dynamics, and human supervision. Robot workload relief is credited only when an eligible service is actually executed, and explicit supervision-load variables deduct the corresponding nurse capacity from clinical coverage. The receding-horizon formulation also includes a cross-window night--morning constraint and a terminal battery reserve. The computational study is presented as numerical verification on synthetic hospital-like instances rather than clinical validation. Under the proposed formulation, the eight-nurse reference case gives $Z_1=0.78$ and $Z_2=3.164$. A common-budget comparison on B20 seed~1 yields total shortage $53.70$ for the integrated model, compared with $58.03$ for sequential nurse--robot scheduling and $59.46$ for the nurse-only baseline. Additional experiments examine multiple epsilon budgets on a larger B30 instance, sensitivity to robot-relief/supervision parameters and objective weights, and one-day versus two-day rolling horizons against a static full-horizon reference. The battery and routing representations remain aggregate planning approximations, and the scalability evidence is interpreted accordingly. No patient records or real hospital staff data are used, so the results establish model behavior and comparative numerical evidence rather than practical clinical effectiveness.

title: Impurity-induced loss bursts from anomalous scale-free localization in a non-Hermitian dissipative lattice
abstract: We identify anomalous scale-free localization and associated impurity-induced loss bursts in a non-Hermitian dissipative cross-stitch lattice. By a local basis rotation, the model is mapped onto an effective non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice, where local impurities act as tunable effective boundaries. For the parameter choice considered here, the impurity-free periodic-boundary-condition point is reached at $η=1$. Tuning $η$ away from this point drives the system through generalized-boundary-condition regimes toward two effective open-boundary-condition-like limits at $η\to0$ and $η\to\infty$. For finite $η\notin\{0,1\}$, the loop-sector spectra remain separated from the real-energy axis, while the corresponding eigenstates exhibit scale-free localization pinned by the impurity. Unlike conventional impurity-induced scale-free localization, the Lyapunov exponent depends explicitly on the eigenenergy, making the localization strength eigenstate dependent. We further show that this anomalous eigenmode structure produces an impurity-induced loss burst: The long-time integrated dissipation probability develops a pronounced local enhancement relative to the surrounding background near an impurity-generated effective boundary, even when the initial wave packet is prepared far away. In the single-impurity case, the burst region consists of the impurity site and its adjacent effective-boundary site, and the effect occurs without imaginary-gap closing. For multiple impurities, local burst regions emerge around all impurities, while the dominant burst boundary is selected by the initial wave-packet position and the nonreciprocal drift direction. These results connect anomalous scale-free localization with controllable dissipation dynamics in non-Hermitian lattices.

title: Meta-Mathematics of Algebraic Complexity
abstract: We initiate the study of the meta-mathematics of algebraic circuit lower bounds, aiming both to gain insight into the methods sufficient and necessary to prove algebraic circuit lower bounds, and to contribute to the study of bounded arithmetic as a logical foundation for complexity lower bounds. We demonstrate that while algebraic circuit lower bounds are hard for somewhat weak proof systems such as Polynomial Calculus Resolution ($\mathsf{PCR}$), contemporary lower bounds are efficiently provable in proof systems and bounded arithmetic theories corresponding to $\mathsf{NC}^2$, such as $\mathsf{VNC}^2$ and the corresponding class of propositional Frege proofs of quasipolynomial-size. Moreover, going below $\mathsf{VNC}^2$ into algebraic constant-depth reasoning is likely insufficient to efficiently prove already constant-depth algebraic circuit lower bounds. Under an algebraic analogue of the Krajicek--Razborov conjecture, our results suggest that proving superpolynomial lower bounds for general algebraic circuits will require stronger reasoning than that used in the rank-based proofs studied here. title: Sharp Asymptotic Minimaxity of the Gavrilov-Benjamini-Sarkar Step-Down Testing Procedure in Sparse Gaussian Sequence Models
abstract: False discovery rate control does not by itself guarantee optimal recovery of sparse signals: a procedure may make few false discoveries while missing an unnecessarily large fraction of the alternatives. We investigate whether the classical Gavrilov--Benjamini--Sarkar (GBS) step-down procedure also achieves the sharp frequentist minimax limits for sparse recovery in independent Gaussian sequence models. Under a beta-min separation at the critical sparse detection boundary, GBS attains the exact asymptotic risk constant $\barΦ(b)$ for normalized Hamming loss and combined $\mathrm{FDP}+\mathrm{FNP}$ loss. The Hamming conclusion remains valid when the number of signals is only bounded above by the nominal sparsity $s_n$. For heterogeneous signal magnitudes, the corresponding risk under either loss equals the sharp benchmark $Λ_n(a)+o(1)$, without assuming that $Λ_n(a)$ converges; this is additive, rather than necessarily relative, sharpness. We assume $s_n\to\infty$, $n/s_n\to\infty$, and a vanishing nominal level $α_n$ satisfying $\log(1/α_n)=o(\sqrt{\log(n/s_n)})$. Unlike step-up rules, a step-down procedure must satisfy every preceding ordered $p$-value constraint before reaching a given rank. Our analysis handles this sequential obstruction directly: a finite-sample shifted order-statistic bound makes false positives negligible, while new uniform crossing arguments show that the rejection path reaches the optimal fraction of signals. The results extend the range of testing architectures known to attain the sharp minimax benchmarks, without requiring localization of a single rejection threshold.

title: Asymptotic Bayes Optimality Under Sparsity of the Gavrilov-Benjamini-Sarkar Step-Down Testing Procedure
abstract: In this article, we investigate the asymptotic Bayes optimality under sparsity (ABOS) of the Gavrilov-Benjamini-Sarkar (GBS) step-down multiple testing procedure (Gavrilov et al., 2009) in the sparse Gaussian sequence model. While the asymptotic optimality properties of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure have been extensively studied, corresponding results for the GBS procedure remain unavailable despite its favorable finite-sample performance in several settings. Within the spike-and-slab Bayesian formulation and the asymptotic decision-theoretic framework of Bogdan et al. (2011), we establish that the GBS procedure is ABOS over a broad class of sparse asymptotic regimes. Existing analyses of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure rely on approximating the random rejection threshold by a suitable deterministic surrogate. In contrast, our approach proceeds through a direct analysis of the Bayes risk by separately controlling the false discovery and false nondiscovery components. The analysis combines two key ingredients: a new finite-sample inequality for shifted order statistics associated with the GBS critical constants and a signal-crossing argument for ordered alternative $p$-values that exploits the sequential step-down structure of the procedure. For diverging expected signal counts, these tools yield ABOS without threshold localization. For bounded positive expected signal counts, a direct argument based on the first GBS critical constant establishes ABOS as well. In particular, our results cover polynomial sparsity $p_m\asymp m^{-β}$ for every fixed $0<β\le1$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first asymptotic decision-theoretic analysis of the GBS procedure and the first proof of its asymptotic Bayes optimality under sparsity.

title: Vib2ECG: A Co-Located Chest-Lead SCG-ECG Dataset and Benchmark for ECG Reconstruction
abstract: Twelve-lead electrocardiography (ECG) is essential for cardiovascular diagnosis, but its long-term acquisition in daily life is constrained by complex and costly hardware. Recent efforts have explored reconstructing ECG from low-cost cardiac vibrational signals such as seismocardiography (SCG), with prior studies primarily focusing on limb leads, while clinical diagnosis requires multi-lead ECG, including chest leads. In this work, we propose Vib2ECG, a dataset of synchronized, co-located ECG and chest-wall vibration recordings, which includes complete twelve-lead ECGs and vibrational signals acquired by inertial measurement units (IMUs) at the six standard precordial electrode sites (V1-V6) from 17 subjects. Based on this dataset, we also provide a benchmark. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of reconstructing electrical cardiac signals at variable locations from vibrational signals using a lightweight 364K-parameter U-Net. Furthermore, we observe a hallucination phenomenon in the model, where ECG waveforms are generated in regions where no corresponding electrical activity is present. We analyze the causes of this phenomenon and propose potential directions for mitigation. This study demonstrates the feasibility of mobile-device-friendly ECG monitoring through chest-lead ECG prediction from low-cost vibrational signals acquired using IMU sensors. It expands the application of cardiac vibrational signals and provides new insights into the spatial relationship between cardiac electrical and mechanical activities with spatial location variation.

title: A Sentinel-2 benchmark dataset for deep-learning active-fire segmentation across 25 California wildfires, July 2020-August 2026
abstract: This article describes an open image dataset for developing and evaluating active-fire segmentation methods in satellite imagery. The dataset contains 2,148 image-mask pairs from 25 California wildfires, with acquisitions spanning July 2020 to August 2026. Each image is a 512x512-pixel, three-channel composite derived from Sentinel-2 Level-2A bands B12, B11 and B8A at 20 m spatial sampling. A fixed linear rendering is applied throughout the dataset. Corresponding masks distinguish background, SWIR-rule active fire and invalid observations. The masks were generated from shortwave-infrared brightness and near-infrared contrast, followed by constrained neighborhood growth. The release includes chip-level metadata and an incident-disjoint partition containing 18 training, three validation and four test fires. Among the image pairs, 841 contain active-fire labels; these labels occupy 0.0766% of all grid cells. A mask-blind analyst review covers 233 test chips and provides a separate assessment of the rule-generated labels at chip and connected-component levels. Reference training and evaluation code accompanies the data, including a ResNet-34 U-Net implementation with validation-based checkpoint and threshold selection. The archived images, masks, metadata and review annotations support research on rare-class segmentation, learning from algorithmic labels and transfer across fire incidents. The versioned dataset is deposited on Zenodo, with preparation and reuse software maintained in a public GitHub repository.

title: All the Facts, Still the Wrong Answer: Integration Gaps in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Multimodal reasoning requires models to combine multiple pieces of evidence into decisions that satisfy all relevant constraints. Evaluations centered on final-answer accuracy leave unclear whether failures arise from reading individual facts or using them together. We study this question through the multi-evidence integration gap, linking local fact recovery to global decision validity on controlled subset-selection and path-finding tasks. Our evaluation combines conditional performance given correct local answers with same-grid local queries, text-oracle inputs, retrieval controls, and constraint ablations. We further examine hidden-state probes and activation replacement across network depth, token positions, and model families. Across the evaluated models, accurate local recovery coexists with substantial global failure. For example, Gemma-3-27B recovers all evaluated isolated item facts correctly but achieves only 19.75% global validity on eight-item visual instances. Probes decode information about solution membership from global-prompt states, while corresponding clean-state replacement recovers failed decisions over model-dependent depth ranges. These findings show that recovering facts and representing solution-related information are insufficient for reliable joint decisions. They motivate evaluations and model improvements that explicitly target how available evidence is combined, alongside advances in perception and model scale.

title: Deep-Microscopic Photonic Bandstructure of a Two-Dimensional Honeycomb Lattice
abstract: Conventional descriptions of light in materials rely on macroscopic models that average the optical response over the microscopic lattice structures. These models are deployed in the semi-classical limit, where the collective local response over many lattice sites is adequate. However, they fail to capture the full spatial dispersion, which requires a lattice-resolved description of light. We address this limitation by formulating a deep-microscopic nonlocal theory of the photon based on the Maxwell Hamiltonian and its characteristic equation. The solution reveals the full spatial dispersion in the form of deep-microscopic photonic bandstructure, and corresponding real-space Bloch field textures. We demonstrate our theory for a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model of a gapped honeycomb lattice. Our framework thus extends photons to the same microscopic footing as electrons or phonons, providing a unified route to studying topology, dissipation, and quantum fluctuations of light in dispersive materials.

title: Beyond Affine Reconstruction: Multi-Resolution Transformer DeepONets for the Radiative Transfer Equation
abstract: Radiative heat transfer plays a dominant role in fire simulations, where solving the radiative transfer equation (RTE) is a computational bottleneck. Neural operators can accelerate these computations by learning solution operators from offline simulation data. However, conventional DeepONet surrogates rely on fixed-grid inputs and affine reconstruction, limiting their flexibility across resolutions and their approximation accuracy at a fixed latent dimension. In this paper, we develop a transformer-based DeepONet for multi-resolution RTE surrogate modelling. The proposed approach combines a Perceiver encoder, which maps temperature and absorption coefficient fields at different spatial resolutions into a fixed-size latent representation, with a cross-attention decoder that enables non-affine reconstruction of the radiative intensity. This architecture allows a single model to process inputs at varying resolutions without resampling them onto a common grid. We formulate a computable empirical version of a previously derived theoretical lower bound for affine reconstruction, enabling direct comparison with model errors on the same dataset. Experiments on a two-dimensional pool-fire dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms autoencoder-based DeepONets in predicting both radiative intensity and incident radiation, with fewer trainable parameters. Power spectral density analysis shows improved preservation of small-scale structures. Both affine baselines remain above the corresponding lower bound at all evaluated ranks, whereas the proposed model achieves a training error below it at one matched latent dimension, demonstrating the potential of non-affine reconstruction to overcome this representational limitation. Experiments on a dataset combining three spatial resolutions confirm the accuracy advantage of the approach at each input resolution.

title: Power-of-Two Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Neurons for Event-Driven Vision-Language-Action Inference
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on dense, continuous-valued computation presents a fundamental challenge for energy-constrained deployment. Inspired by the sparse, event-driven signaling and temporal integration mechanisms of biological neurons, a promising alternative is to introduce spiking computation into VLA models. However, enabling such computation without restructuring pretrained policies or compromising closed-loop control remains an open challenge. To address this challenge, we introduce the Power-of-Two Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (PoT-LIF) neuron, which emits signed spikes with power-of-two amplitudes. By combining magnitude-coded spike events with residual-preserving membrane dynamics, PoT-LIF enables continuous information to be progressively represented through discrete spikes. The Heartbeat formulation further localizes this process within weighted projections, bridging biologically inspired spiking computation and pretrained VLA architectures without modifying their external inference interfaces. We integrate PoT-LIF into the vision projection, vision-language projection, and action projection of $π_{0.5}$ and evaluate both operating modes over 2,000 paired closed-loop LIBERO episodes per configuration. Standard-mode PoT-LIF VLA achieves success rates of 96.90% and 96.35% at $T = 1$ and $T = 2$, respectively, while Heartbeat mode achieves 97.25% and 96.90% at $T = 2$ and $T = 4$, compared with 96.70% for the original continuous-activation $π_{0.5}$ baseline. At $T = 1$ with a 60.01% firing rate, PoT-LIF uses approximately 1/7.67 of the dense-reference arithmetic energy, corresponding to a modeled reduction of 86.95%.

title: Structure-Preserving Numerical Schemes for a Time-Fractional Porous Medium Equation with Nonlocal Pressure
abstract: In this work, we study numerical approximations of the equation \begin{equation} \partial_t^αu-\nabla\cdot\left(u^{m-1}\nabla(-Δ)^{-σ}u\right)=0, \end{equation} where $0<α<1$, $0<σ<1$ and $m>1$. The Caputo derivative is discretized by the L1 formula, while the nonlinear nonlocal flux is approximated by a conservative upwind finite-difference scheme. We establish several structural properties of the implicit scheme in arbitrary space dimension, including a discrete maximum principle, non-negativity, mass conservation, $\ell^\infty$ and $\ell^2$ stability, existence of non-negative discrete solutions, and a discrete energy-dissipation estimate. Our assumptions include natural symmetry, a sign condition on the sum of the directional coefficients, and decay on the discrete weights. We also derive a consistency estimate for the complete nonlinear spatial operator. For rigorous convergence analysis, we restrict ourselves to one space dimension and introduce the cumulative variable associated with the density. This transforms the discrete problem into a monotone approximation of an equation involving the fractional Laplacian. Interestingly, for semigroup-based pressure-gradient weights, the resulting discrete operator is identified with the fractional discrete Laplacian. Next, using comparison and contraction properties of the integrated scheme, for $m\geq2$ and under the stated spatial regularity and weighted temporal consistency assumptions, we prove uniform convergence of the cumulative numerical solution and convergence of the corresponding density against compactly supported smooth test functions. The temporal estimates allow a weak singularity at the initial time. We also analyze an explicit variant of the scheme and derive a sufficient CFL condition covering the full range $0<σ<1$.

title: End-to-end prostate lesion segmentation and detection from undersampled diffusion-weighted MRI
abstract: Automated prostate lesion detection from diffusion-weighted MR imaging (DWI) conventionally relies on reconstructed images and does not fully use all acquisition information. We present an end-to-end network that uses complex multicoil DWI data and coil sensitivity information for prostate lesion segmentation. We included 269 fastMRI prostate examinations with additional voxel-level lesion annotations. Of these, 64 examinations contained PIRADS 4 or 5 lesions. The proposed network, VarNet-Seg, consists of a k-space variational network (VarNet) with six variational cascades and an image-space 3D segmentation U-Net. Comparator models used the same segmentation architecture with fully coil-combined images (CC-Seg), fixed root-sum-of-squares reconstruction (RSS-Seg), or fixed SENSE reconstruction (SENSE-Seg). We performed ablations with end-to-end training and data consistency (DC) enabled or disabled. We evaluated lesion segmentation using Dice and patient-level detection using AUROC in five-fold cross-validation with full sampling, simulated undersampling, added noise, or both. VarNet-Seg achieved the highest Dice at every undersampling level. At eight-fold acceleration, Dice was 0.22 for VarNet-Seg, 0.14 for SENSE-Seg and 0.16 for VarNet-Seg (no DC). The paired difference from SENSE-Seg was 0.08 (95% CI, 0.04-0.11). With full sampling, VarNet-Seg and RSS-Seg performed similarly (0.40 vs 0.39). Patient-level AUROC decreased from 0.75 with full sampling to 0.63 at eight-fold acceleration; corresponding RSS-Seg AUROCs were 0.76 and 0.64. The proposed multicoil network improved prostate lesion segmentation under simulated undersampling compared to conventional models. Matched ablations supported contributions from both end-to-end training and data consistency. Prospective evaluation is needed to establish whether this approach can be used clinically in accelerated prostate DWI.

title: A Density--Delay Law for Event-Driven State Progression in Open Distributed Systems
abstract: This paper studies delay-induced competition in an honest event-driven longest-chain network and distinguishes selected-tip divergence from lowest-common-ancestor (LCA) competing-branch depth. With density--delay load \(x_N=λΔ_{\max}\), regenerative analysis gives the explicit network-size-uniform bound \(μ_N(x_N)\le e^{2x_N}+e^{x_N}-2\) on proposal-clock mean LCA depth. Bounded \(x_N\) suffices for this guarantee. At fixed delay, \(g(N)=O(1/N)\) is one corresponding input-rate scaling. An explicit finite-horizon depth-exceedance bound is also established. Explicit-node simulations show strong load effects and comparatively small finite-size effects. The results concern honest contention, not adversarial security.

title: Large spin large deviations for interacting particle systems
abstract: We propose a novel framework for analyzing the sample-path large deviations of interacting particle systems directly on a lattice by considering a large-spin limit ($s \to \infty$). Through an appropriate scaling of variables, the process concentrates around its deterministic trajectory, governed by the lattice diffusion equation. We quantify the exponential cost of observing atypical trajectories by explicitly computing the path-space large deviation rate function from the scaled microscopic generator, based on a theory due to Feng and Kurtz. The rate function is described in terms of a Hamiltonian on a lattice in terms of classical spin variables. Notably, for our main model, the symmetric harmonic process, the corresponding Hamiltonian is identified with the classical integrable non-compact Ishimori spin chain. Furthermore, we show that our large spin large deviation theory is fully consistent with traditional Macroscopic Fluctuation Theory (MFT), smoothly recovering the standard MFT Hamiltonian in the spatial continuous limit. We also perform a Poisson-noise Martin--Siggia--Rose (MSR) computation to derive the non-linear lattice Hamiltonian directly from microscopic dynamics, use a relative entropy argument to obtain the density-current action, and establish the lattice fluctuation theorem alongside its symmetry origin. Overall, our framework provides a naturally regularized, lattice analogue of MFT that circumvents spatial ultraviolet singularities and possible continuous density blow-ups. We also apply our new scheme to partial symmetric exclusion process, symmetric inclusion processes, Brownian energy process and integrable heat conduction model, showing how their large-deviation Hamiltonians relate to classical compact and non-compact spin chains.

title: Five Architectures, One Shared Space Cross-Model Representational Alignment Without Weight Merging
abstract: Combining language models is usually done by averaging weights, which works only when the models share a common starting point. We ask whether five frozen, independently trained models with different internal designs (four transformers from four organizations and one state-space model) can be related through their activations alone, with no weight merging. Using permutation tests, an independent replication probe set, depth sweeps, pooling ablations and confound checks, we find statistically robust correspondence between how the five models organize the same text. It is strongest at each model's final layer and weaker for the state-space model, whose weakest pairing is still 35-43 times chance. We use this to build a shared space with Generalized Procrustes Analysis, in which no model is a fixed reference. At the final layer, mean held-out retrieval accuracy over the twenty ordered model pairs is 0.91 to 0.93 on two probe sets (chance 0.03), beating pairwise linear maps (0.82 to 0.85), but the space is worse than those maps in the middle layers. It transfers to ordinary English of unfamiliar grammatical form and fails on mathematical and logical notation. We then test whether the space supports a router that picks among the five models on gradeable tasks. Across four task types we find no case where routing beats always using the strongest model, and we report this as a negative result. A correctness signal that looked strong turned out to be category membership in disguise. All experiments ran on one laptop without a GPU.

title: HI3D 3.0 (Twinkle3D): Object-specific 3D Asset Generation with High Resolution
abstract: Image-to-3D generation has become increasingly capable of producing objects that closely resemble the input image, and an outstanding challenge is to reproduce the depicted object itself, including the specific geometry that defines it. Inscriptions, brand marks, and repeated structures are frequently distorted or lost, despite being critical to object identity. We present Hi3D 3.0, an image-to-3D generation system targeting object-specific fidelity, with Twinkle3D as its geometry model for generating watertight triangle meshes at $2048^{3}$ resolution. Twinkle3D advances high-fidelity geometry generation along four dimensions. First, while O-Voxel/FaithC offers high representational precision, it often suffers from poor surface quality and non-watertight geometry. We address both issues while retaining its $2048^{3}$-level precision. Second, we scale diffusion generation to sequences of up to 300K geometric tokens through a redesigned DiT architecture and large-scale distributed training optimizations, reducing training time per step from approximately ten minutes to ten seconds. Third, subsequent refinement cannot fully compensate for errors introduced during initial generation; we therefore strengthen both global shape and local detail in the initial generation stage, and the resulting single-stage model surpasses prior two-stage pipelines with $512^{3}$ refinement. Finally, we introduce a fine-grained image-3D cross-modal interaction mechanism that strengthens correspondence between visual evidence and geometric tokens, improving the recovery of object-specific structures. We evaluate geometric fidelity using alignment metrics derived from silhouettes and normal fields. Hi3D 3.0 outperforms four commercial systems across all reported metrics, recovering 82.1% of inscribed characters at 98.2% precision, compared with 21.7% recall for the strongest competitor.

title: MS-COOT: Comparing Morse-Smale Complexes with Co-Optimal Transport
abstract: Understanding and comparing structures in scalar fields is a central challenge in scientific visualization, with applications ranging from feature analysis to temporal and structural comparison. The Morse-Smale (MS) complex provides a natural representation by decomposing a scalar field into regions induced by gradient flow. However, existing approaches typically rely on graph-based representations, matching critical points without explicitly establishing correspondences between regions. In this work, we represent the MS complex as a hypergraph, where critical points form nodes and regions define hyperedges. We introduce MS-COOT, a co-optimal transport distance that jointly computes correspondences between critical points and regions. This formulation enables explicit region-to-region matching within a distance-based framework, allowing identification of region-level events such as splitting and merging. We instantiate this framework with domain-specific components, including a hypernetwork function encoding relationships between critical points and regions, persistence-based probability measures, and a sample cost term that incorporates critical point attributes. We evaluate MS-COOT on datasets spanning 2D simulations, 3D surface meshes, and volumetric data. Our results show that MS-COOT provides distinct characterization of certain region-level structural changes compared to graph-based distances, achieves competitive accuracy in shape classification, and improves classification of simulation parameter settings in a 3D ensemble.

title: Real Time Motion Detection in Video Inspired by Photonic Time Stretch
abstract: Motion perception is fundamental to computer vision and physical AI, and plays a central role in robotics, autonomous vehicles, human-computer interaction, and video compression. Traditional approaches such as background subtraction, frame-differencing and optical flow algorithms often struggle in complex or dynamic scenes, typically sacrificing spatial resolution for computational tractability. Here we introduce MoViD (Motion estimation via Virtual dispersion and phase Detection), a physics-inspired algorithm grounded in the principles that govern photonic time stretch - a highly successful ultrafast realtime data acquisition platform. Drawing inspiration from the optical physics therein, MoViD treats video as a collection of optical time series waveforms associated with pixels. Motion of an object through a pixel broadens the time series spectrum and, after group delay dispersion, induces a temporal phase that exists only if there is motion. Spatiotemporal group delay dispersion templates, corresponding to dielectric functions, classify specific motion trajectories. Unlike conventional empirical phase-based motion-analysis pipelines that require narrow-band spatial channelization and pyramid reconstruction, the physics-based MoViD operates directly on the broadband video signal, vastly increasing its computational speed. The resulting algorithm achieves unprecedented performance in both motion characterization and motion magnification, providing full-resolution motion mapping in real time at nearly 200 frames per second at 4K resolution and 70 frames per second for 8K video - orders of magnitude faster than classical optical flow approaches or learning-based methods. Notably, such extreme performance enables real time motion analysis at ultrahigh resolution for motion detection and compensation in robotics and other autonomous devices.

title: Junction Hook Errors in the Color Code
abstract: Color-dependent syndrome extraction schedules have been proposed to mitigate hook errors in the triangular color code. Recent work by Kishony and Fowler (arXiv:2603.28852) identifies distance-reducing hook errors by the type of anyon for which they provide a shortcut and chooses the CNOT ordering for stabilizers of each color to avoid these errors. We identify an additional class of distance-reducing hooks, which we call junction hook errors, that is not captured by this classification. The two data qubits of a junction hook error terminate anyon strings of two different colors at the point where the three colored strings of a logical operator meet, which we call the junction. As such, the hook error does not correspond to a single type of anyon, yet it still reduces the distance. For distances $d=7,9,11$, we verify that every non-corner plaquette admits a scheduled hook error that, together with $d-2$ single data qubit faults, produces an undetectable logical error using $d-1$ faults. Each of these is a junction hook error. Because of this, every stabilizer, including those in the bulk, still requires additional protection from hook errors (such as flag qubits) to restore the full circuit-level distance with this schedule. A minimum weight logical operator has at most one junction, however, so junction hook errors cannot accumulate on one minimum weight logical operator in the way that single-color malign hook errors can. This helps explain why the schedule still improves the circuit-level distance to $d-\lfloor (d+3)/6\rfloor$, rather than the $d/2$ distance associated with spatially uniform color code scheduling.

title: Stability of certain elements in the Bernstein center
abstract: Let $G$ be a split connected reductive algebraic group over a non-archimedean local field $F$ of characteristic zero. The stable center conjecture asserts that the subspace of stable elements in the Bernstein center of $G(F)$ is a sub-algebra, and this subring is conjecturally isomorphic to the regular functions on the moduli of semi-simple Langlands parameters. Bezrukavnikov-Kazhdan-Varshavsky suggested an approach towards the stable center conjecture by explicitly constructing elements and proving their stability directly without assuming LLC, and proved the stability of the depth-$r$ projectors. Following the idea, the first author and Tsao-Hsien Chen produced a family of elements in the center which are conjecturally stable using Deligne-Lusztig parameters attached to irreducible representations. This paper proves the stability of the projectors corresponding to strongly regular Deligne-Lusztig parameters in depth-zero, and for all the positive depth elements with some restrictions on the residue characteristic.

title: Wasserstein convergence rates for empirical measures of point processes
abstract: In this paper, we establish upper and lower bounds on the convergence rate of empirical measures of point processes under the Wasserstein distance. To this end, we first introduce a new metric on the space of finite counting measures. Unlike many existing metrics in the literature, our proposed metric incorporates the spatial locations of unmatched points. Drawing on both this new metric and existing metrics from the literature, we identify a set of common structural properties and develop a general framework for Wasserstein distances between point-process distributions based on metrics satisfying these properties. We then use this framework to investigate the convergence rates of empirical measures, providing quantitative guarantees for approximating the distribution of the underlying point process, and further establish corresponding concentration inequalities. These theoretical results may provide ingredients for constructing oracle goodness-of-fit tests for a specified point-process distribution. We also apply our theory to the approximation of Campbell measures and discuss how the resulting bounds can help assess Wasserstein-based learning of generative point-process models.

title: Optimal Search Strategies under Finite Resource Constraints
abstract: Improving target search is a challenge faced by many natural and artificial agents, often requiring the use of energetic or material resources. These inputs may be supplied by an external controller or generated by the searcher itself, for example, through the deposition of cues along its trajectory. Although such resources are commonly modeled as costly but available without an explicit limit, in practice, they can often only be produced in finite amounts. Here, we go beyond the assumption of an unlimited supply of resources by investigating searches in which a finite resource budget must be allocated throughout the search process. To investigate this problem, we equip a one-dimensional diffusive searcher with three types of resources: an external force, a supply of partially reflecting flags, and auto-chemotactic cues. We derive exact optimal resource-allocation protocols for informed search processes in which the agent has continuous access to its past and current positions, which we find to always require resource allocation to be spatially concentrated. We then determine the corresponding protocols for blind searchers and show that resource usage must be more evenly distributed. Non-Markovian cues that generate environmental memory are found to substantially improve search performance when the agent has access to positional information, even under finite-resource constraints. In contrast, their benefits are considerably more limited for blind search, particularly when the cues provide no directional information.

title: VitronEdit: Universal Visual Editing across Images, Videos, and 3D Scenes
abstract: Recent advances in unified visual editing have begun to consolidate image and video editing within a single model, while 3D scene editing remains largely separate and constrained by scarce paired training data. Given the rich image and video editing supervision now available and the common editing semantics shared across modalities, a natural question is whether this knowledge can be transferred to data-scarce 3D editing. We present VitronEdit, a universal framework for image, video, and 3D scene editing. VitronEdit adopts a shared sequence representation and progressive multimodal training to transfer editing knowledge across modalities. We further introduce geometry-aware post-training, which leverages a pretrained geometry reconstruction model to provide depth and camera-pose supervision. Surprisingly, applying geometric supervision only to 3D samples yields the best overall performance, while image and video editing also improve despite receiving no direct geometric supervision, suggesting that geometric regularization transfers through the shared backbone. Our analysis further shows that image and video training mainly transfers editing semantics to 3D, whereas 3D supervision primarily improves multi-view consistency. The project page: https://vitron-llm.github.io/VitronEdit/.

title: IMU4D: 4D Human-Object Understanding from Wearable IMUs
abstract: Understanding human activities and the objects they interact with typically relies on visual perception, yet cameras pose persistent challenges in privacy, safety, energy efficiency, and scalability. We explore an alternative: 4D perception without vision. Its goal is to recover human motion and the objects the person interacts with purely from everyday wearable sensors. For this we introduce IMU4D, a framework that repurposes large language models for non-visual spatiotemporal understanding of human-object dynamics. IMU4D uses data from a few inertial sensors from earbuds, watches, or smartphones and predicts detailed 4D human motion together with surrounding objects the person interacts with. Experiments across diverse human motion datasets and human-object datasets show that IMU4D yields more coherent and temporally stable results than SoTA cascaded pipelines, suggesting wearable motion sensors alone can support 4D understanding of human-object interactions.

title: AV-FABLE: Audio-Visual Manipulation Forensics in Long-Form Videos
abstract: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. We introduce AV-FABLE, a dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE contains 16,650 pristine--manipulated twin pairs (998 hours) created with 27 editing configurations, with separate audio and visual timelines that enable modality-specific temporal localization and expose errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. On AV-FABLE, zero-shot prompting of audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) yields near-chance detection and poor temporal localization. In contrast, supervised readouts of their frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, suggesting manipulation evidence is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs. Motivated by this observation, we propose NFSR(Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which reads frozen AV-LLM features with separate audio and visual temporal decoders. NFSR achieves the best audio-visual localization performance in-domain and across all three out-of-distribution settings, including transfer to held-out videos from an external long-video forensic benchmark. AV-FABLE, code, and model weights will be publicly released.

title: WorldCast: World-Consistent Character Video Generation with Large-Angle Camera Control
abstract: Precise camera control is essential for cinematic character video generation, yet existing methods struggle to follow large-angle trajectories with combined rotation, translation, and radius variation from arbitrary initial azimuths. Such viewpoint changes also reveal character regions unseen in the initial frame, causing geometric distortions, appearance degradation, and identity drift. To systematically study these coupled challenges, we introduce CLACT, a large-scale Character-centric dataset and benchmark covering diverse Large-Angle Camera Trajectories, with accurate camera geometry and multi-view character observations for training and evaluation. We further propose WorldCast, a framework for world-consistent character video generation under diverse large-angle camera motions. Specifically, we back-project the initial frame into a 3D point cloud using estimated depth, align the point-cloud scale with the target camera trajectory, and render it along the trajectory to obtain explicit geometric guidance and coverage masks. To complement the incomplete character information, we introduce Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA). Using relative camera poses estimated jointly from the initial frame and multi-view character anchors, we express anchor and target-view geometry in a common coordinate frame. GAMA uses this geometric alignment to guide the retrieval and injection of view-relevant character features during generation. Evaluations across diverse large-angle camera trajectories demonstrate accurate trajectory following while preserving character geometry, appearance, and identity.

title: WorldMirror: Agentic Real-to-Sim Generation of Interactive Worlds from In-the-Wild Robot Demonstrations
abstract: Existing approaches for robot learning in simulation often require substantial manual effort to construct scenes and specify tasks, limiting training scalability and data diversity. Meanwhile, in-the-wild robot demonstrations naturally provide diverse and realistic observations of real-world interactions. Leveraging these demonstrations for simulation requires both high-fidelity visual reconstruction and physically consistent interactions. General-purpose agents offer flexible adaptation to diverse scenarios and strong reasoning about 3D spatial relationships, while specialized generative models provide high-fidelity reconstruction of scene appearance and geometry. We introduce WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework that constructs interactive digital twins from in-the-wild robot demonstrations. Our central idea is to formulate real-to-sim construction as the iterative refinement of an executable world program. A coding agent decomposes the observed scene, plans reconstruction steps, and orchestrates specialized image and 3D generation tools, refining the program through verification feedback. A camera-pose-anchored scene representation organizes the world into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships among the scene, objects, and robot. The agent uses this representation to diagnose and correct reconstruction errors, enabling physically consistent interaction and trajectory replay. Experiments on DROID demonstrate that WorldMirror can reconstruct visually faithful and geometrically consistent interactive worlds while preserving the physical validity of recorded robot trajectories.

title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?
abstract: Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents on active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout.

title: TKCAM: Text and Keyframe to Camera Trajectory Generation
abstract: Generating high-quality and controllable camera motion is essential for AI-assisted cinematography, video synthesis, and 3D scene understanding. We introduce TKCAM, a Text- and Keyframe-conditioned CAMera-motion synthesis framework based on generative masked modeling. We represent camera dynamics using a 12-dimensional kinematic feature comprising position, velocity, and a continuous rotation representation and discretize them into hierarchical motion tokens via a Residual Vector Quantizer (RVQ). A two-stage masked transformer architecture then learns to reconstruct and refine these tokens, utilizing explicit self- and cross-attention modules for multimodal conditioning. A central feature of our framework is sparse visual keyframe conditioning: users can provide free-form text prompts together with RGB observations at selected timestamps, which provide temporally localized visual guidance for generating coherent in-between trajectories. Furthermore, to advance evaluation standards, we curate RealEstate10K-Cap, a large-scale text-camera dataset, and establish a cross-domain benchmark with a Universal CLaTr Evaluator. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TKCAM surpasses recent state-of-the-art baselines on Fréchet distance (FID), text-motion matching scores, and retrieval metrics (R@K), while additional analyses evaluate temporal smoothness and cross-domain generalization. Code and RealEstate10K-Cap dataset are available at https://github.com/linearalgebrayhz/TKCAM.

title: From Events to Enhancement: A Survey on Event-Based Imaging Technologies
abstract: Event cameras offering high dynamic range and low latency have emerged as disruptive technologies in imaging. Despite growing research on leveraging these benefits for different imaging tasks, a comprehensive study of recently advances and challenges are still lacking. This limits the broader understanding of how to utilize events in universal imaging applications. In this survey, we first introduce a physical model and the characteristics of different event sensors as the foundation. Following this, we highlight the advancement and interaction of image/video enhancement tasks with events. Additionally, we explore advanced tasks, which capture richer light information with events, \eg~light field estimation, multi-view generation, and photometric. Finally, we discuss new challenges and open questions offering a perspective for this rapidly evolving field. More continuously updated resources are at this link: https://github.com/yunfanLu/Awesome-Event-Imaging

title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but pursues a proxy that coincided with the intended goal during training instead of the goal itself. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents and what enables them to be recovered without retraining. We study this across eight visual navigation and manipulation tasks, including robot control. While tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, we uncover that the goal is lost at one of three different depths. This depth predicts which recovery works in each task. When the goal is followed, but outcompeted by the proxy, steering the existing policy redirects it to the goal's location, raising goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. When it is read, but not followed, steering fails, but a lightweight new downstream wiring recovers goal reach from 31.6% to 84.3%. When it is not read, none of the methods work, as the policy does not use the goal information. The same tracing also reveals what replaces the goal: functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, or cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. Knowing where the goal is lost tells us whether an agent can be repaired or has to be retrained. Goal misgeneralization should therefore be studied and evaluated inside the agent, not only from its behavior.

title: MvT: Event-based Multi-view Projection for Multiple Object Tracking
abstract: Event cameras are increasingly used for Multiple Object Tracking (MOT), but their asynchronous event output often requires specialized methods. Existing processing methods primarily follow two paradigms, pseudo-frames and event-by-event. The former is the prevailing approach since its data format aligns with images, making image-based techniques applicable. However, it suffers from tracking failures when trajectories overlap or are spatially close on pseudo-frames. Facing this challenge, we propose a multi-view pipeline, Multi-view Tracking (MvT), which preserves the 2D data format to leverage image-based techniques directly while introducing additional spatio-temporal views to resolve tracking ambiguities in a single view. MvT comprises a Multi-view Projection (MvP) module and a Multi-view Fusion (MvF) stage. MvP encodes events into three complementary spatio-temporal views while mitigating the pattern discretization. Within MvF, multi-view results are unified into a 3D coordinate system, and tracklets are associated through an optimization model subject to specific criteria combination. Evaluations on four datasets, including our self-collected Small Objects Dataset (SOD), show that MvT seamlessly integrates image-based methods and outperforms existing non-learning and learning trackers in generalized scenarios, and effectively resolves the single-view tracking ambiguities. Being training-free, MvT is applicable when ground-truth annotation is infeasible, thereby highlighting its practical, data-efficient potential. Code is available at https://github.com/zhazhabiu/MvTracking.

title: On the Theory of Bias Tuning in Event Cameras
abstract: This paper lays the foundation of a theory for bias tuning in neuromorphic cameras, a novel sensing technology also known as "event cameras". We begin by formulating the high-level effect of the sensitivity biases on the camera's event rate in mathematical terms. We then show that, as a corollary of the Poincare-Miranda theorem, the commonly used tuning principles of rate budgeting and polarity balancing lead to a unique configuration of the sensitivity biases. As a corollary, we show how by adopting these principles, the multi-variable bias-tuning problem reduces to a two-parameter problem that can be resolved experimentally.
